title: Bounded intersection-preserving replacement for a set of presheaf monomorphisms
statement:
Fix an input universe $\mathcal U$ as in [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $A$ be a $\mathcal U$-small ordinary category, $\mathcal P=\operatorname{Fun}(A^{\mathrm{op}},\operatorname{Set}_{\mathcal U})$, $B$ any presheaf in $\mathcal P$, and $\Lambda$ a $\mathcal U$-small set of monomorphisms in $\mathcal P$. Let $\operatorname{wsat}(\Lambda)$ denote closure under isomorphisms, pushouts, $\mathcal U$-small transfinite compositions continuous at limits, and retracts in the arrow category. A presheaf $Z$ is $\Lambda$-injective if every map $D\to Z$ extends to $E\to Z$ for every $(D\hookrightarrow E)\in\Lambda$. Write $|F|=|\coprod_{a\in\operatorname{Ob}(A)}F(a)|$ for total-element size.

There exist an endofunctor $R:\mathcal P\to\mathcal P$, a natural transformation $\eta:\mathrm{id}\to R$, and infinite regular cardinals $\lambda<\alpha$ in $\mathcal U$, with $\alpha>|\operatorname{Mor}(A)|$ and $\alpha>|B|$, having all the following properties. Regular means that a union of fewer than the cardinal many sets, each of smaller cardinality, still has smaller cardinality.

(1) Each $\eta_F:F\to R(F)$ belongs to $\operatorname{wsat}(\Lambda)$, and $R(F)$ is $\Lambda$-injective.

(2) The functor $R$ preserves monomorphisms. For any subpresheaves $S,T\subseteq Y$, identify their $R$-images with subpresheaves of $R(Y)$. The canonical map identifies $R(S\cap T)$ with $R(S)\cap R(T)$.

(3) If $|F|<\alpha$, then $|R(F)|<\alpha$ and $|B\times R(F)|<\alpha$.

(4) For every $Y$, the union of $R(T)\subseteq R(Y)$ over all subpresheaves $T\subseteq Y$ with $|T|<\alpha$ is $R(Y)$.

(5) For every increasing family $(T_\xi)_{\xi<\lambda}$ of subpresheaves of $Y$, indexed by the initial ordinal of cardinality $\lambda$, the canonical map identifies $\bigcup_{\xi<\lambda}R(T_\xi)$ with $R(\bigcup_{\xi<\lambda}T_\xi)$ as subpresheaves of $R(Y)$. All these constructions and colimits remain in $\mathcal U$.

source.place: Cisinski, Higher Categories and Homotopical Algebra, construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65 (PDF pp. 79-80). Agent formulation with separate preservation rank lambda and larger size bound alpha, so lambda < alpha; the source gives preservation of sufficiently long unions and small supports. The fixed auxiliary B only increases the size bound. Read online 2026-10-17, not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this arbitrary-set small-object replacement with intersection and cardinal controls.

proof.text: Write the generators as $i:D_i\hookrightarrow E_i$, indexed by the small set $\Lambda$. Apply [lem-coef-small-family-regular-bound] to the small family consisting of $\mathbf N$, $\operatorname{Mor}(A)$, $\Lambda$, and the total-element sets of all $D_i,E_i$. Obtain an infinite regular cardinal $\lambda$ strictly greater than every one of these sizes. Fix this cardinal independently of the input presheaf. All Hom sets of presheaves are small: a natural transformation is a family of functions indexed by the small object set, satisfying equations indexed by the small arrow set. In particular the set of pairs $(i,u)$ with $u:D_i\to F$ is small for every $F$.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text:
Small presheaf colimits are computed objectwise. Indeed form at each $a$ the quotient of the disjoint union of the values of a small diagram by its arrow relations. Restrictions send relations to relations and hence descend; the functor laws hold on representatives. Compatible maps to any presheaf descend uniquely at each object, and their uniqueness proves naturality. This verifies exactly the colimit universal property of [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. For a presheaf $F$ form
$$S(F)=\coprod_{(i,u:D_i\to F)}D_i,\qquad C(F)=\coprod_{(i,u:D_i\to F)}E_i,\qquad Q(F)=F\amalg_{S(F)}C(F),$$
where $S(F)\to F$ evaluates $u$ and $S(F)\to C(F)$ is the coproduct of the $i$. Denote the first pushout leg by $q_F:F\to Q(F)$.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text:
We first check the elementwise meaning of a monomorphism: for $a\in A$ let $h_a(b)=\operatorname{Hom}_A(b,a)$ with restrictions by composition. An element $d\in D(a)$ defines a natural map $h_a\to D$, taking $g:b\to a$ to $D(g)(d)$. If $i_a(d)=i_a(d')$, these two maps have equal composites with $i$ by naturality, so monicity makes them equal; evaluation at $1_a$ gives $d=d'$. Conversely componentwise injections cancel any two natural transformations componentwise and hence are monomorphisms. Thus all generator components are injective. Because each $i$ is injective objectwise, the quotient realizing the colimit universal property [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit] for this pushout has the following bijective normal form at every object $a$:
$$Q(F)(a)=F(a)\amalg\coprod_{(i,u:D_i\to F)}\big(E_i(a)\setminus i(D_i(a))\big).$$
To verify it, send an old element to its first-summand value, send $(i,u,i(d))$ to $u(d)$, and keep every $(i,u,e)$ with $e$ outside the image as its own distinct new symbol. These maps identify exactly the pushout relations and give mutually inverse maps of the quotient and the displayed set. Restrictions of new symbols use restriction in $E_i$; if that restriction lands in $i(D_i)$, use its unique preimage and then $u$. Thus $q_F$ is a monomorphism. For $f:F\to G$, send old $x$ to $f(x)$ and new $(i,u,e)$ to $(i,fu,e)$. This respects the quotient relations and restrictions, gives $Q(f)$, and proves identity, composition and $Q(f)q_F=q_Gf$ directly.

proof.text: If $f$ is monic, $u\mapsto fu$ is injective, so the normal form in Step 3 makes $Q(f)$ injective at every object. For $S,T\subseteq Y$, the old elements in both $Q(S)$ and $Q(T)$ are exactly $S\cap T$. A new symbol $(i,u,e)$ of $Q(Y)(a)$ is in $Q(S)$ precisely when $u$ factors through $S$, and similarly for $T$. Both factorizations exist precisely when every component value of $u$ lies in $S\cap T$; these component maps then give the unique natural factorization through $S\cap T$. Hence the common new symbols are exactly those of $Q(S\cap T)$. Old symbols never equal new ones. This proves both monomorphism preservation and preservation of intersections for the one-step functor, including empty domains and empty intersections.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: Use [lem-weil-pbc-transfinite-recursion] on the small ordinal $\lambda+1$ to construct functors $F_\beta$ and compatible natural transition maps for $0\leq\beta\leq\lambda$: $F_0=\mathrm{id}$, $F_{\beta+1}=QF_\beta$, and $F_\delta(F)=\varinjlim_{\beta<\delta}F_\beta(F)$ at every nonzero limit $\delta$. The successor transition is $q_{F_\beta(F)}$; all earlier transitions are its composites. At a limit the transition maps are the coprojections of the objectwise colimit of Step 2. For a morphism $f$, use $Q(F_\beta(f))$ at successors and the map induced by the colimit cocone at limits. The successor functor laws follow from Step 3; the limit laws follow because the two maps agree after every coprojection. The same checks give naturality of all transitions and their composite identities. This specifies the recursion on coherent prefixes; give any fixed dummy output on an incoherent prefix, and the displayed induction shows it is never used. Set $R=F_\lambda$ and let $\eta:F_0\to F_\lambda$ be the natural transition.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: Transfinite induction shows all transition maps are monic, each $F_\beta$ preserves monomorphisms, and $F_\beta(S\cap T)=F_\beta(S)\cap F_\beta(T)$ inside $F_\beta(Y)$. The successor assertions follow from Steps 3-4 applied to the already monic images at the previous stage. At a nonzero limit all transitions are injective, so the objectwise colimit is their union: the equivalence relation generated by transitions identifies two representatives precisely when they become equal at a common later stage: a finite zigzag of transition identifications has an upper bound below the limit, where all its equalities hold. This quotient is the colimit of [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit], by Step 2. This also makes the induced map for a monomorphism injective, since equality can be tested at that stage. An element in both limiting images of $S$ and $T$ has representatives at two stages; pass to a common stage below the limit at which their images in the ambient chain agree, where the inductive intersection assertion puts it in the image for $S\cap T$. The reverse inclusion follows from the two inclusions. This proves (2) for $R$ and also justifies all subobject identifications below.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: Each $q_F$ belongs to $\operatorname{wsat}(\Lambda)$. Well-order its small attaching set $(i,u)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-well-ordering-theorem], with small ordinal order type $\rho$. For $\gamma\leq\rho$ let $P_\gamma$ be the pushout attaching only the copies indexed by ordinals $<\gamma$, using their original maps to $F$. Then $P_0=F$, each successor $P_\gamma\to P_{\gamma+1}$ is a pushout of the single generator indexed by $\gamma$, and the diagram is continuous at limits. These assertions follow from the universal property in [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]: a map out of any such stage is a map out of $F$ and one map out of each attached $E_i$ agreeing with $u$ on its $D_i$; at a limit this is precisely a compatible family of the preceding data. The final stage is the simultaneous pushout $Q(F)$ by the same test. Weak saturation therefore gives $q_F$, including the isomorphism when the attaching set is empty. The continuous $\lambda$-chain defining $\eta_F$ consists of these maps, so closure under small transfinite compositions gives $\eta_F\in\operatorname{wsat}(\Lambda)$.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: For $i:D_i\hookrightarrow E_i$ and $u:D_i\to R(F)$, choose for every total element of $D_i$ a stage $\beta<\lambda$ representing its image. There are fewer than $\lambda$ elements, so regularity gives one $\beta<\lambda$ containing all their images. Since $F_\beta(F)\hookrightarrow R(F)$ is monic, $u$ factors uniquely as a natural map $u_\beta:D_i\to F_\beta(F)$: restrictions agree after this monomorphism and hence before it. The copy of $E_i$ labelled by $(i,u_\beta)$ at the next attachment supplies an extension $E_i\to F_{\beta+1}(F)\to R(F)$. The initial ordinal of the infinite cardinal $\lambda$ is a limit, so $\beta+1<\lambda$. This proves $\Lambda$-injectivity and completes (1). The stage choices are legitimate: well-order $\lambda$ and take each least representing stage.

proof.text: If $|F|<\alpha$ then $|F|\leq\mu$. Whenever $|H|\leq\mu$, a natural transformation $D_i\to H$ is determined by its function on total elements, so there are at most $\mu^{|D_i|}\leq\mu^\theta=\mu$ choices (the empty domain gives one choice). The normal form of Step 3 therefore gives $|Q(H)|\leq\mu$: there are $|\Lambda|<\lambda\leq\theta<\mu$ generator indices, at most $\mu$ attaching maps for each index, and each $E_i$ has size $<\lambda$, so the set of new total symbols injects into a product of three sets of size at most $\mu$. At a limit $\delta\leq\lambda$, the union of at most $\lambda\leq\mu$ total-element sets of size at most $\mu$ again has size at most $\mu$. Transfinite induction gives $|R(F)|\leq\mu<\alpha$. Finally the total-element set of $B\times R(F)$ injects into the product of the two total-element sets (retain the common object label), so it too has size at most $\mu\mu=\mu<\alpha$. This is (3).

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: For every $\beta\leq\lambda$, every $a\in A$, every $Y$, and every $z\in F_\beta(Y)(a)$, prove by transfinite induction the support assertion: there exists a subpresheaf $T\subseteq Y$ of total size $<\lambda$ such that $z$ lies in $F_\beta(T)(a)\subseteq F_\beta(Y)(a)$. At $\beta=0$, take the subpresheaf generated by $z$; its total elements are restrictions of $z$ along arrows with target $a$, so its size is at most $|\operatorname{Mor}(A)|<\lambda$. At a limit $\beta$, $z$ has a representative at an earlier stage; its supporting subpresheaf remains a support after the transition. For the successor induction assume the assertion at $\beta$ simultaneously for all objects and elements. If $z$ is an old element, its existing support works. If it is a new symbol $(i,u,e)$, for each total element $d$ of $D_i$ choose a support $T_d$ for $u(d)\in F_\beta(Y)$. Such choices can be made by well-ordering the small set of subpresheaves of $Y$ (coded by subsets of its total-element set) and taking the least suitable support for each $d$, using [lem-weil-pbc-well-ordering-theorem]. Put $T=\bigcup_d T_d$. There are fewer than $\lambda$ choices, each of size $<\lambda$, so regularity gives $|T|<\lambda$. Each $u(d)$ then lies in $F_\beta(T)$ by functoriality and Step 6. The monic inclusion $F_\beta(T)\hookrightarrow F_\beta(Y)$ ensures these component values give a natural map $u_T:D_i\to F_\beta(T)$. The symbol $(i,u_T,e)$ of $QF_\beta(T)$ maps to $z$. This completes the induction, including $D_i=\varnothing$, where $T=\varnothing$.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: Apply the support assertion at $\beta=\lambda$. Every total element of $R(Y)$ belongs to $R(T)$ for a subpresheaf $T\subseteq Y$ of size $<\lambda<\alpha$. Conversely every such image is a subpresheaf of $R(Y)$ by (2). Their objectwise union is therefore exactly $R(Y)$, proving (4). This is an actual small union: the subpresheaves of $Y$ form a subset of the power set of its total-element set.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: For (5) put $V=\bigcup_{\xi<\lambda}T_\xi\subseteq Y$. Any $z\in R(V)(a)$ has, by Step 11 applied with $V$ in place of $Y$, a support $S\subseteq V$ of size $<\lambda$. Every total element of $S$ lies in some $T_\xi$. Choose its least such ordinal; fewer than $\lambda$ ordinals have been chosen, so regularity bounds them by one $\xi<\lambda$ (use $0$ when $S$ is empty). Hence $S\subseteq T_\xi$ as subpresheaves. Functoriality puts $z$ in the image of $R(T_\xi)$ in $R(V)$ and then in $R(Y)$. The reverse inclusion follows from $T_\xi\subseteq V$. Since $R$ preserves monomorphisms, this is exactly the canonical identification of the stated union with $R(V)$, rather than just a noncanonical bijection.

source.place: Construction 2.4.36 and Lemma 2.4.37, printed pp. 64-65; agent supplies the omitted details.

proof.text: All presheaf values, Hom sets, attaching sets, objectwise quotients and power sets above belong to $\mathcal U$. All recursion and colimit indices are small ordinals in $\mathcal U$: the fixed $\lambda$-iteration and the well-orders of the small attaching sets. The cardinal constructions use small disjoint unions, power sets and successor cardinals in $\mathcal U$. Grothendieck-universe closure in [def-weil-size-convention] thus keeps every construction and colimit in the input universe. The resulting single $R,\eta,\lambda,\alpha$ satisfy all five clauses simultaneously, with no assumption on the size of $Y$ other than its membership in $\mathcal P$. To compare with the source size convention, define $A/F$ to have objects $(a,x)$ with $x\in F(a)$, and an arrow $(a,x)\to(b,y)$ to be $g:a\to b$ with $F(g)(y)=x$. Identity arrows embed the total-element set of $F$ in $\operatorname{Mor}(A/F)$, and an arrow is determined by $(g,y)$, giving $|F|\leq|\operatorname{Mor}(A/F)|\leq|\operatorname{Mor}(A)|\cdot|F|$. Since $\alpha$ is infinite and $|\operatorname{Mor}(A)|<\alpha$, the counting argument of Step 9 makes the two size-below-$\alpha$ conventions equivalent, including $F=\varnothing$.
